en: *Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra: Explaining the Two "Wei" (For) Chapters*, composed by Ji of Daci'en Monastery.
In order to analyze the two "wei" chapters, they shall briefly be distinguished by way of five gates: first, manifesting the fixed number of sounds; second, based upon... [text continues].

The "Explanation of the Fixed Number of Syllables" (*Shengding xun*) consists of three parts. The second part, the "Explanation of the Sequence of Syllables," is divided into seven sections according to the different numerical divisions of the scriptures, totaling seven fascicles.
Fifth, it sets forth the author’s intent.

First, it clarifies the fixed number of syllables; there are two types: (1) the number of single characters and (2) the fixed number of syllables. Taken as a whole across the entire collection, there are six hundred and one [syllables].
There are eighteen characters and two hundred and ninety-one characters. Of these, three hundred and twenty-seven are in the level (ping) tones and sixty-four are in the departing (qu) tones.

Regarding the second section, which determines the meanings based on tone: those in the level tones have nine meanings (*yōng* [phonetic transcription for *yǒu*]): "to have," "to follow," "to seek," "to obtain," "to determine," "to be subjected to," "to act," "to be," and "to name.
Those in the departing tones have three meanings (*yōng* [phonetic transcription for *yì*]): "to take," "to give," and "to assist."

Third, regarding the sequence of phonetic explanations (*śabdavyutpatti*): it is simply that wherever a particular sound occurs at the beginning of a sutra, one explains its meaning according to that sound as the sequential order.

In this way, the phonetic explanations from beginning to end do not become confused. Furthermore, a single phrase is often cited universally so that the text may be clear and the meaning manifest, making it easy to find upon investigation;
these may appear at the beginning, middle, or end. Within this context, if it is the same as the usual [practice], [it follows the standard].

I call upon you simply to instruct me; if you deviate from what was previously stated, I shall certainly speak again. Please reflect upon the meaning and ensure it accords with broad learning and virtuous wisdom;
I humbly request that you examine this in detail.
Fourth, regarding the classification of the scriptures.

○ In the Introductory Chapter, he constantly acts for the sake of all Buddhas (attaining), for the sake of all Bodhisattvas (bestowing two), preaches Nirvana (bestowing), preaches Pratyekabuddhahood (bestowing),
preaches the Pure Path (bestowing), and lectures on the Dharma for the assembly (bestowing), yet does not take pride in these; this is making offerings to the śarīra.
Is this intended to be taught as a meditative concentration (*samādhi*), or is it intended to be given as a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*)? What kind of concentration is to be taught?

Is it for those seeking the state of a śrāvaka, or for those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha? It is for the sake of acting as a Dharma-preacher; it is for the sake of providing the necessary causes and conditions;

it is for the sake of expounding the teaching for others; it is for the sake of extensive analysis; it is for the sake of being the eye of the world; and it is for the sake of speaking it for you all.
It is said: "To purify the body" (this is the name); it is called "seeking fame" (one should act to sever and eliminate this).
The above, from the first category, consists of twenty-three characters: nine in the level tone and fourteen in the departing tone.
Regarding the matters of the "Expedient Means" chapter: shall the Buddha explain them? Is this the ultimate [teaching], or is it the definitive practice?
Is it spoken according to reality? For the sake of the Buddha’s eldest son and for this assembly, I shall now speak for you.
I shall now explain for you that which all Buddhas always perform as a single task: they preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
All these teachings are for the sake of [sentient beings], and thus they preach the Dharma; in this way, all of it is for the sake of [them].
This teaching of Nirvana takes the Mahāyāna as its foundation; for the sake of these Buddhas, they preach the Mahāyāna.
Regarding these matters, [the Buddha] spoke of the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and spoke of skillful means (*upāya*). Whether it was for the sake of building a stupa for the Buddha,

or for the sake of people regarding the truth as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), regarding the truth as the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*), regarding them as sentient beings, regarding them as all sentient beings,
regarding the teaching of bodhisattvas, regarding the five bhikṣus, or for the sake of speaking of the Buddha’s wisdom— [all were done through skillful means].
This constitutes having already made offerings; this constitutes [offering] to the Kings of All Dharmas; this constitutes [giving] to such as these.
The above is the second chapter: forty characters, ten characters in the level tone, and thirty characters in the departing tone.
The Parable Chapter: [Is this] for self-deception? Is it for all together? Is it not so? Is it for the sake of the various brahmins? Is it the work of Māra?
Is it that which is attained by devas and humans? Is it for the sake of the unsurpassed path? Is it for the sake of the śrāvakas? [It is] made with lapis lazuli as the ground.
Using gold for cords, because it is a great treasure, [it is named] *Heng* (Constant). For the sake of all Buddhas, he attained [enlightenment];
while serving as a prince, he served under Buddha Guangfo (Light Buddha) and made a vow: "For the sake of the fourfold assembly, may they all attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
In order to transform bodhisattvas, even when being burned by fire, I shall preach the Dharma for them so that they do not suffer from the fire."
What is this that is called a "house"? What is meant by "loss"? This house has already been, and will certainly be, consumed by fire;
it is not something false. It is that which has already been attained, and it is all things.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, one does not regard birth, old age, and sickness as afflictions. I am for the sake of sentient beings; [I act] for the sake of all sentient beings.
For those within the three realms who have been taught the Three Vehicles, and for those who are being burned—I now act for your sake.

For those seeking the sheep or the deer, I am called Mahā-; for all the multitudes who are oppressed by fire and about to be destroyed by it, I provide for you a cushion and a mat, and am able to provide protection and refuge.
I act for the sake of sentient beings; for those who are unsurpassed, and for their sake, I take desire as the root.
For the sake of the Truth of Cessation, this is called liberation. Having attained the status of Dharma King, I act out of a desire to benefit them;
thus they shall see me. This is the teaching for those of profound wisdom; it should not be taught to others.
Furthermore, for those who have been born as children, or as small insects, or even if they obtain human birth,

being made to serve others as their servants or being used as clothing— only for such as these may you preach [the Dharma]. For the sake of attaining all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), you should preach it to them.
The above is the third chapter, consisting of eighty-one characters: forty-six in the level tone (*ping sheng*) and thirty-five in the departing tone (*qu sheng*).
○ The Chapter on Faith and Understanding (*Xinjie pin*).
What is it that, when perceived and grasped, is called "son" (putra)? It is named "child" (dāraka). This is not different from our being sons;
this is what we consider sufficient. It is not through discrimination that one becomes a Bodhisattva.
To the Buddhas, he is as a son; to the Kings, he is as a constant attendant. He acts to eliminate defilements and takes pleasure in humble tasks.

Whether for the sake of great bodhisattvas, or for bodhisattvas alone, or for those who do not seek [the goal] for themselves but consider themselves sufficient in having attained the untainted and unconditioned— having already attained these—
they may be of inferior capacity; yet, according to what is appropriate, they preach the Dharma for them.
The above constitutes the fourth chapter, consisting of twenty-four characters: ten in the even tone (ping sheng) and fourteen in the departing tone (qu sheng).
○ In the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter, [the Buddha] preaches the Dharma for the sake of hearing it; he does not preach immediately [upon their arrival], which is most rare. Is it? Yes.
This would be a permanent loss [of the opportunity] for me to teach according to their capacities, for all sentient beings, for myself as a Tathāgata,
for myself as a World-Honored One, to speak for the great assembly, always for the great assembly,
constantly for all, as if for a single person, and to be called the Great Tree; it is for your sakes that I do so now.
The above is the fifth chapter. Fifteen characters: five in the level tone (ping sheng) and ten in the departing tone (qu sheng).
○ Chapter on Bestowing Prophecy: Attaining Buddhahood (3). The ground is made of lapis lazuli (2). Gold serves as the cords (2). [It is] for the sake of Buddha-wisdom (1).
They manifest as adornments, they bestow predictions of enlightenment, they create crystal grounds, and they preach the Dharma for the multitudes;
all these are for the sake of attaining the Buddha-way throughout the ten directions, so that they may eternally serve gods and humans.
The above is the sixth chapter. Eleven characters are in the level (ping) tone; five characters are in the departing (qu) tone.
○ In the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter:
grind it to make ink (as); exhaust the powder to make dust (as two); take all of it to make ink (as); and let the dust represent one kalpa (as).

First, for the sake of those Buddhas; second, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddhas; third, for the sake of delivering sentient beings; fourth, for the sake of attaining the greatest [attainment];

fifth, one should vow for the sake of the world; sixth, for the sake of manifesting through discernment; seventh, for the sake of the assembly of Brahmās; eighth, for the sake of attaining the great heavens—these four;

ninth, for the sake of the appearance of Buddhas in the world—these four; tenth, for the sake of acting as a creator for sentient beings; eleventh, for the sake of acting as [the protector] of sentient beings; twelfth, for the sake of acting as the eye of the world.
When he was a śrāmaṇera, he preached this sutra for our sake and for the sake of the fourfold assembly; it is most rare that he acted thus as a member of the retinue.
When he was a śrāmaṇera, he preached this sutra for these reasons and for the sake of bringing rest. Now, for your sake, he does so likewise for the sake of bringing rest.
I have taught for you, I have awakened the multitudes for you, I have proclaimed various things for you,

and I have done so for immeasurable billions of times; I have also acted for you as a guide for all, teaching the cessation that is Nirvana, and teaching the truth— now I act for you as the Buddha for all.
The above is the seventh chapter, consisting of fifty-two characters: twenty-two in the level tone (*ping sheng*) and thirty-one in the departing tone (*qu sheng*).
○ Chapter on the Five Hundred Disciples.
Performing what is rare, he shall preach the Dharma; attaining the foremost [state], he shall purify a Buddha-field.
Manifesting the foremost [state], he shall make that single Buddha-field have the seven treasures for its ground. Seeking the Unsurpassed, his name shall be Ratnaprabhāsa (Jewel Radiance).
These shall constitute the Saṃgha; when he becomes a Buddha, his title shall be Samantaprabhāsa (Universal Radiance).

I shall now proclaim for you that those who take little wisdom as sufficient, doing so merely for the sake of food and clothing, and regarding such things as sufficient—asking "what else is needed for food and clothing?"—are exceedingly deluded.

When one was a bodhisattva, having attained a small measure [of realization], one took that as sufficient; yet you claim this is self-sufficiency, taking a mere trifle as sufficient, thinking it to be true extinction.
The above is the eighth chapter. Twenty-five characters and eighteen characters are in the level (ping) tone; seven characters are in the departing (qu) tone.

○ The "Chapter on Human Remembrance" and others [state that] for all [beings], he is a constant attendant (serving as such), the ground is made of lapis lazuli, and he becomes a Buddha throughout the ten directions.
Acting as an attendant through skillful means, he served all Buddhas; he also served this Buddha when that Buddha was a crown prince.

He acted as Rāhula, the eldest son, receiving the Dharma for the sake of the Dharma. He served as their elder in all these roles, manifesting as my own elder, whose name is Reality-Character (Svabhāva-lakṣaṇa).
The above, from the ninth chapter, consists of thirteen characters and eleven characters in the level (ping) tone, with two characters in the departing (qu) tone.
○ In the "Dharma Master" chapter:
"To secretly [teach] for one person (with 'and') / Or to widely preach for many people (with 'and') / Is to act as a Tathāgata (attaining two) / And is the most difficult to believe (is)."
To explain it for others is to provide them with robes;

to reveal and elucidate it for those in other regions, one should know that this is called providing for the fourfold assembly, acting on behalf of the fourfold assembly, providing for all bodhisattvas, and for their assembled listeners. I shall further explain it for them and analyze it in detail.
Taking compassion as one’s chamber and the emptiness of phenomena as one’s seat, this is for the purpose of teaching, for teaching it to sentient beings,
for providing them protection, for manifesting it at that time, for explaining it now universally, for teaching it to the fourfold assembly,
and for providing them with the opportunity to hear the Dharma.
The above, from the tenth chapter, consists of twenty-six characters in the even tone and sixteen characters in the departing tone.
○ The "Treasure Stūpa" chapter serves as an adornment; it is for the sake of preaching to the great assembly, for the sake of listening to this sūtra, and for the sake of providing witness.

For the sake of hearing the Lotus Sutra, they take crystal for the ground (and construct it) as an adornment; for the sake of preaching the Dharma to the assembly, they take lapis lazuli for the ground (and construct it);
with yellow for the cords (and construct them), they act as attendants (and construct them) as adornments.
They serve as a single Buddha (and construct them), and they serve all Buddhas when (and with) they hear this sutra; even if they have come for the sake of the Dharma, (they do so) for this purpose.
To not be diligent for the sake of the Dharma, yet to sit before all Buddhas as an act of making offerings;
to do so for the sake of this sutra, thereby seeing me—this would be a difficult task. Yet even that is not yet difficult; it is not yet considered difficult.
To expound this to the multitude—that indeed is difficult. To expound it for others and to establish me in the Buddha-way.
This constitutes the swift attainment [of the goal].
The above, from the eleventh chapter, consists of forty-five characters: thirty are level tones (ping sheng) and sixteen are departing tones (qu sheng).
Chapter on Deva:
Desiring to fulfill [the purpose], for the sake of the Dharma, who is able to act for me? One should proclaim it;
one should prepare a seat; seeking the Great Dharma, one should explain it for me; one should act as a servant.
I shall speak for you, for the sake of all sentient beings, and not for my own sake; I shall speak as one who has become a great king,
for your sake and extensively for the sake of sentient beings— for the sake of sentient beings, universally for the ten directions,
and universally for this assembled congregation.
The above, Chapter Twelve, consists of eighteen characters: three characters are in the level (ping) tone, and fifteen characters are in the departing (qu) tone.
○ Chapter on Exhorting to Uphold.
Do not harbor such concerns; [this] is for the sake of being a great Dharma Master (or: both as Dharma Masters). May you not harbor such concerns.
When you have not yet attained [it], do not claim to have attained it. This is how you will be honored by the world. Do not act out of greed for gain and offerings, nor for the sake of seeking fame.
It is for these reasons that you have encountered this, and it is for these reasons that you preach this sutra.
The above is the thirteenth chapter. Eleven characters and eight characters are in the level (ping) tone; three characters are in the departing (qu) tone.

○ The Chapter on Peaceful Practices (*Anle-xing-pin*) is extremely rare to encounter. (This is) being able to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings (and) thus preaching the Dharma for them (two).
To act with intimacy and affection; to act for the sake of women, even for the sake of the Dharma, or for the sake of hearing the Buddha-way;
to kill for the sake of profit; to preach the Dharma for the sake of women—these are called the conditioned and the unconditioned.
To provide explanations for various kings, to speak according to their questions, and to speak with a serene countenance.
Not to speak much is a great loss; these two are for the sake of always being a bhikṣu, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, and for the sake of always [upholding] the Dharma.
To speak various sūtras and yet not speak [them], to be a Great Dharma King—this is most profound.
To speak this Dharma is to be able to perform a difficult task, [acting as] a king of all dharmas.
For the sake of these sentient beings—and for this sūtra as the most honored—this has been spoken for you to serve as attendants;

it is for the Buddha’s sake, and for the fourfold assembly, and for the purpose of making offerings. It is to grant them the prediction of enlightenment, so that they may hear the Dharma and speak it for others, and for the sake of the fourfold assembly.
The above is the fourteenth chapter; it contains forty-four characters: seventeen in the level tone (*ping sheng*) and twenty-seven in the departing tone (*qu sheng*).
○ Chapter on the Emanation of Rays.
Who is this foremost one? From what meditative concentration does he come? Who is it that speaks this?
For the sake of seeking the Buddha-way, when he was a crown prince, for the sake of the Buddha-way—this is most rare; we pray you will explain it.
To remove the doubts of the multitude, the Buddha explains it both for the future and for the present.

The above is the fifteenth chapter. Thirteen characters are level tones (ping sheng), and nine characters are departing tones (qu sheng). ○ In the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*), Maitreya is the leader;
[the Buddha] takes the atoms at the beginning and end as minute particles (*paramāṇu*); he exhausts them to form dust, and grants this prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) for such a person.
All for the sake of liberation; (1) for the sake of delivering sentient beings; (2) for those struck by poison; (3) for the sake of sentient beings;
(4) for the sake of preaching the Unsurpassed; (5) not for the sake of manifesting his own body; (6) then appearing to preach for this assembly; (7) for the sake of preaching the rarity of a Buddha;
(8) for the sake of treating the mad son; (9) likewise for the sake of worldly people; (10) for the sake of the delusions of ordinary folk.
He preached various [teachings] (and gave).
The above, the sixteenth chapter, consists of eighteen characters: five in the level tone and thirteen in the departing tone.
○ Chapter on the Differentiation of Merit:
To be thus slighted by others for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is to obtain merit such as this;

it is to see the Buddha, it is to possess deep faith, and it is to bear [the Dharma] upon one’s head. It is not necessary to build a stūpa for me; this itself constitutes having already built a stūpa.
To have already [realized] that there is no [self] is to establish [the truth]; to explain it to others is to give it to others;
and to give it to others is to fulfill it. As described above, this is to be in accord with liberation and to perform that which is untainted and unconditioned.
The seventeen chapters above contain nineteen characters in the level (ping) tone and six characters in the departing (qu) tone.
○ In the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing," for how much [merit] shall one act as a parent for their kin? Is it not much? It is for the sake of this sutra.
One distinguishes it for others, rejoices in it for others, explains it through skillful means for others, attains that which is beyond analogy,
and gains what is cherished by people.
The above is the eighteenth chapter. [The rhyme scheme is: nine characters and four characters in the level tone (ping sheng), and five characters in the departing tone (qu sheng).
○ *Fǎshī Gōngdé Pǐn* (Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma-Master): "If for others" (yú èr); "for the Trāyastriṃśa devas" (yú); "if for others to preach" (yú); "or for people to preach" (yú).
For the sake of hearing the Dharma, sometimes for the purpose of manifesting it, for the purpose of preaching it to sentient beings, and for the purpose of [benefiting] all the multitudes.
The nine characters above, from the nineteenth chapter, are to be pronounced with the departing tone (rising tone).

In the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging," for the sake of devas and humans, for those seeking the vehicle of śrāvakas, for those seeking the vehicle of pratyekabuddhas, for the sake of explaining the bodhisattva path,
and for the sake of the one named "Never-Disparaging," he extensively preached it to others; he acted for their benefit, and for the sake of the fourfold assembly.
For the sake of explaining it to others (and) for the sake of explaining it to people (and) furthermore for the sake of all people.
The above is the twentieth chapter; eleven characters are level tones and ten are departing tones.
The Chapter on Supernatural Powers was composed for the sake of entrusting [the teaching] to the bodhisattvas, to gladden sentient beings, to assist those seeking the Buddha-way,
and for those who have already seen me.
The above constitutes the twenty-first chapter; the five characters are in the level (even) tones, and the four characters are in the departing (falling) tone.
○ In the "Chapter on Entrustment," one should expound [the teaching] for the sake of causing that person to thereby fulfill their debt of gratitude.
The above is the twenty-second chapter. Three characters are level tone (ping shēng), and two characters are departing tone (qù shēng).
○ In the "Bhaiṣajyarāja" Chapter:
using the seven treasures as a platform (zhì zuò) to make offerings (yǐ wéi gòng yǎng); for the sake of all beings (wèi yī qiè); he immediately becomes their father (jí wéi qí fù).
Sandalwood is the foremost among [accumulations]; the ocean is the foremost, being the most profound and vast;
the mountain is the foremost, being the highest, the supreme, the very first, the most illuminating, and the most venerable.
The Buddha is the foremost, he is also the foremost, and the Bodhisattvas are the foremost; they are the kings of all dharmas.
No longer acting out of greed, nor out of anger, nor out of pride, but speaking for others and giving to them—
this constitutes [the practice of] Jambudvīpa.
The above is the twenty-third chapter. [It contains] twenty-three characters and twenty-one characters in the level tone, with three characters in the departing tone.
○ Chapter on the Wondrous Sound (Ghoṣadatta).
For the sake of immeasurable beings, he preached the Dharma for them; with five *tandula*-gold stems, silver leaves, and diamond filaments, he fashioned a pedestal.
"May it be for us," "it shall be for you," "may it be able to provide offerings"—for the sake of all sentient beings, he transformed into a female body and manifested his form.
The above is the twenty-fourth chapter, consisting of twenty-one characters: nine in the level (ping) tone and twelve in the departing (qu) tone.
○ Chapter on Avalokiteśvara.
If one is swept away by great waters (or rescued from them), or seeks gold and silver, or acts for the sake of sentient beings, or preaches the Dharma to them (nineteen);
if one bestows fearlessness, or acts as Avalokiteśvara, I shall briefly [protect] you; if one is pushed by others (or oppressed), I shall act as a refuge and protector.
The above constitutes the twenty-fifth chapter. [It consists of] twenty-seven characters in the level (ping) tone and twenty-two characters in the departing (qu) tone.
○ Chapter on Dhāraṇī.
Is it not rather that this constitutes an offense and a violation? Furthermore, it also constitutes protection and compassionate regard.
The above is the twenty-sixth chapter: six characters of even tone, four characters of even tone, and two characters of departing tone.
○ Chapter on King Śūra:
Manifesting spiritual transformations; for whom is the Teacher? (Is it for us? For our father; preaching the Dharma for the king.
In order to initiate [the practice].
The above, Chapter Twenty-seven, consists of five characters with one level tone and four departing tones.
○ The Chapter on Samantabhadra.
It is called "Expounding" (to), "Being Protected by All Buddhas" (attaining), "Being Possessed by Māra" (being afflicted), and also "Making Offerings" (by means of).

It is called "Turning the Dharma-Wheel" (this), and "Expounding the Dharma" (to). It is not "Being [Afflicted] by Women" (being afflicted), but "Being [Attained] by All Tathāgatas" (attaining), "Being Empowered by a Thousand Buddhas" (attaining), and "Being [Empowered] by Śākyamuni" (attaining two).
It is not "Being [Afflicted] by the Three Poisons" (being afflicted), nor is it "Being [Afflicted] by Lust and Jealousy."
The above is the twenty-eighth chapter, consisting of one hundred and thirteen characters:

ten in the level tone (ping sheng) and three in the departing tone (qu sheng), totaling six hundred and eighteen characters (two hundred and ninety-one characters in the level tone and three hundred and twenty-seven characters in the departing tone).
Fifth, regarding the general application of the term *manasikāra* (mental attention): this section provides a comprehensive explanation of the essential principles of the five gates.

Fearing that one might follow the ancients by restricting the term’s phonetic transcription to "zuò" (作) or "pèi" (被) alone without grasping its other etymological interpretations, I have set forth these explanations so that future generations who have not yet awakened to them may understand the origins of these glosses.
One must clearly discern the essentials of the Buddha’s word—namely, the nine meanings, the three meanings, the One Vehicle, and the Five Vehicles.
This is stated because it explains the essence of the Dharma through parables.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
